title: Cringe is dead
gist: Lucy Hicks Beach argues 'cringe' has stopped functioning as a social enforcement mechanism: the UK government announced Andy Burnham's premiership with a Love Island-voiceover TikTok and almost nobody reacted. Her causal account is that the internet erased the 'lanes' cringe policed, while a decade of macro crises made small social rules feel trivial — judgement itself is undiminished, only its target has moved.

insights.claim: The UK government announced Andy Burnham's arrival as prime minister with a TikTok using a Love Island voiceover over shoes entering Downing Street, soundtracked by Mabel's 'Don't Call Me Up'.
insights.so_what: Official state communication has fully adopted entertainment-platform grammar, which changes where political attention and persuasion budgets go.
insights.quote: This week,” the recognisable ITV voice says as we see two black shoes walk into Downing Street, “a hot new bombshell enters the villa.
insights.locator: The day Andy Burnham became our latest prime minister
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: The Welsh government joined in the comments with a Love Island catchphrase in Welsh, showing institutional meme participation is now horizontal across government, not a single account's stunt.
insights.so_what: When institutional meme fluency becomes the norm rather than the exception, it stops conferring any differentiating attention advantage.
insights.quote: Croeso. Can I pull you for a chat?
insights.locator: In the comments, the Welsh government chimed in
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Despite coverage by The Times and The Observer, the prime-ministerial TikTok drew almost no public response — the null reaction is the article's central evidence.
insights.so_what: Absence of backlash is now the informative signal; measuring outrage that did not happen is a better read on norm shifts than measuring outrage that did.
insights.quote: Yet, apart from a few murmurs in the comments section, the TikTok went largely unacknowledged.
insights.locator: Other commenters lapped up this notably flippant
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

themes.theme: Cringe as a decayed enforcement mechanism

insights.claim: The key move is separating behaviour from reaction: politicians have not become less embarrassing, but cringe has lost its power as a social enforcement mechanism.
insights.so_what: Reputational sanction is weakening as a constraint on public figures, which lowers the expected cost of erratic or undignified political conduct.
insights.quote: Politicians haven’t become less embarrassing. Instead, somewhere along the line, the idea of what’s cringe has lost its power as a social enforcement mechanism.
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Cringe only functions where there are clear expectations about how different categories of people should behave — the joke depends on the premise that some people are meant to stay in their lane.
insights.so_what: A reusable model: shame-based enforcement requires legible role boundaries, so any domain that loses role clarity loses shame as a control.
insights.quote: Cringe only means something when there are clear expectations about how different people should behave.
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Universal institutional meme adoption — supermarkets doing teen TikTok dances, police forces replying with reaction GIFs, fast-food chains trading banter — has worn the shock off boundary violation entirely.
insights.so_what: Brand social strategies built on transgressive relatability have exhausted their edge; differentiation now has to come from somewhere else.
insights.locator: The internet has steadily eroded those lanes
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Previous eras enforced boundaries harshly — Theresa May's conference dance produced months of memes, Ed Balls Day still commemorates a self-name tweet, Ed Miliband's bacon sandwich endures — establishing how much the sanction has weakened.
insights.so_what: A concrete before/after baseline: the same category of behaviour that once carried months of reputational damage now carries none.
insights.quote: When Theresa May danced at the Tory Party conference, the memes lasted for months.
insights.locator: The internet used to punish people
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: The author ranks prime ministers by what they could have survived — Sunak perhaps, Truss surely not, Boris played the fool actively, and Theresa May doing this content would have caused outcry — implying the shift happened within a single political cycle.
insights.so_what: Dates the norm collapse to roughly the last few years, which matters for anyone modelling how quickly reputational regimes can flip.
insights.locator: It’s hard to put a finger on the timeline
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: The performance itself has not become more sincere — audiences have simply become desensitised, so authenticity signals no longer distinguish anything.
insights.so_what: Desensitisation, not improvement, explains rising tolerance — a warning against reading calm audience response as approval.
insights.quote: The performance hasn’t become any less contrived; we’ve simply become desensitised to it.
insights.locator: Yet, now, awkwardness has become more ordinary
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Years of compounding crises — pandemics, war, climate deterioration, the rise of the far right, economic insecurity and democratic instability — have distorted the sense of proportion that made small social transgressions register as important.
insights.so_what: A general mechanism linking macro volatility to norm decay: crisis saturation devalues the entire tier of minor social rules.
insights.quote: When the foundations themselves appear temporary, the social rules built on top of them begin to feel less important too.
insights.locator: The internet is not the only thing
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: For younger cohorts the instability was concrete rather than abstract — schools closing overnight during Covid, suspended social milestones, a no-longer-assumed liveable climate, overturned US reproductive rights, and receding home ownership and economic security.
insights.so_what: Explains why the cohort discount on institutional continuity is generational and durable, not a phase that reverses with the cycle.
insights.quote: The structures that were supposed to provide continuity have repeatedly disappeared or been challenged.
insights.locator: For younger generations, this instability has not been abstract
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Gen Z's mockery of 'millennial optimism' targets the belief that the right lifestyle and online persona could produce stability — the joke is about a lost world where authenticity was still achievable.
insights.so_what: The collapse of belief that personal branding produces security undercuts an entire creator-economy and lifestyle-marketing premise.
insights.quote: The joke is not simply that millennials were embarrassing; it is that they belonged to an internet where authenticity still seemed like something you could achieve.
insights.locator: Gen Z often mock what they call “millennial optimism”
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: Judgement has not softened — it has redirected: online comments still savage looks, parenting and politics, the Telegraph still runs pieces like 'Why Jameela Jamil is the most annoying woman on the internet', and governments are mocked and distrusted as enthusiastically as ever.
insights.so_what: Blocks the comforting reading that culture has grown kinder — the same aggression is simply pointed at different targets, so reputational risk has moved rather than fallen.
insights.quote: We haven’t, of course, become less judgemental. Certainly not any kinder.
insights.locator: We haven’t, of course, become less judgemental
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach

insights.claim: The government TikTok escaped notice because it was unremarkable rather than clever or authentic — institutional internet-speak is now the baseline expectation, so its execution quality is irrelevant.
insights.so_what: Institutional social content has commoditised: it no longer buys goodwill or attention, only avoids the cost of absence.
insights.quote: It was merely another institution speaking in the language of the internet.
insights.locator: What has changed is the object of that ridicule
insights.speaker: Lucy Hicks Beach
